title: Former UNH star Jerry Azumah celebrated during Homecoming weekend - Seacoastonline.com
content: DURHAM – It seems ludicrous now, but Jerry Azumah didn’t have much to show potential college recruiters when he was in high school because he didn’t get much playing time during his first three years. However, he had a breakout season as a senior at St. Peter-Marian in Worcester, Mass., to justify the University of New Hampshire football program’s keen interest in him. “We had a powerhouse football team at St. Peter-Marian for several years and I never really got to see the football field because we had so many great guys,” Azumah said. “So I just had to wait for my turn. It was all about seniority. Once your time is called you’ve got to make sure that you’re ready. “I was finally going to be the starter and that we were still a really good team and if I got the ball I was going to make teams pay,” he added. “There was no question about that when we saw him on tape,” said former UNH coach Bill Bowes. “I was quite surprised to be honest with you that there weren’t more people recruiting him.” As the featured running back, Azumah averaged almost 10 yards per carry that season. A somewhat hidden gem, he went on to become the Wildcats’ all-time leading rusher and received numerous accolades along the way. The latest and most prestigious one came Saturday afternoon before the start of the UNH football team’s Homecoming game against Elon - a 30-23 win for the Wildcats. That’s when Azumah was presented with a plaque from the National Football Foundation Hall of Fame during an On-Campus-Salute at midfield. He joined Bowes, a 2016 inductee. “It’s amazing, finally, my kids think I’m cool,” Azumah said with a laugh. “Personally, I think Jerry Azumah is the best football player that played at the University the University of New Hampshire, in my opinion,” Bowes said. Azumah, who rewrote the UNH rushing record book, was the first player in Division I-AA/FCS history to rush for more than 1,000 yards in four consecutive seasons, and in 1998 was the recipient of the prestigious Walter Payton Award as the top offensive player in the country. The ceremony was held at the ESPN Zone in New York City’s Times Square. “UNH really embraced me and I really appreciated that,” Azumah said. “Football is the ultimate team sport. Yes, I got the accolades and awards and things like that but I needed so much help from the coaching staff, to the (athletic) trainers, to the guys on the football field. Ultimately, those are the things that helped propel me forward. I couldn’t have done them all by myself.” During his four-year tenure Azumah set two FCS records with 6,193 career rushing yards and 8,376 all-purpose yards. Azumah holds multiple school records, including rushing yards in a game (329) and a season (2,195), and touchdowns for a career with 60. He averaged about 6 yards per carry for his college career which included a four-year total of 1,045 carries. “He carried the ball a lot during his tenure at the University of New Hampshire,” Bowes said. “He never missed a game. I don’t recall him ever having to come out of the game for any length of time because of injury. For a running back that’s a lot to be said, particularly ones like him that are carrying the ball so much.” Azumah demonstrated his physical attributes by rushing for more than 100 yards in 25 of 41 career games at UNH. As a senior workhorse in 1998 he gained 2,195 yards on 343 carries and averaged 247.8 all-purpose yards per game, eclipsing 200 yards five times. “A little bit of luck and good coaching as well,” Azumah said of his ability to stay on the field. “I tried to make sure I maintained a strong body and a strong mind, and tried to do the necessary things that it took to make sure that my body could endure the punishment and never break down. “I just wanted to get an opportunity to play,” he added. “That was my only expectation and once I got that opportunity I believed in myself and knew that my talents would take over.” Tony Trisciani, Elon’s head coach, was the running backs coach at UNH when Azumah burst on the scene in the late 1990s. “He was awesome,” Trisciani said, “a relentless competitor, extremely talented, great teammate and human being. You could see the talent, the ability, the explosiveness he had as an athlete and a competitor. He was fun to coach. It was an awesome experience. I’m glad I had that opportunity with him”. Elon’s Kamerin McDowell-Moore rushed for 273 yards and two touchdowns Saturday against UNH. “That was an Azumah-like performance,” Trisciani said. “Probably hasn’t been anybody run like that on this field since No. 25.” After showcasing his durability in college where he helped lead the Wildcats to two Atlantic-10 New England Division titles, Azumah demonstrated his versatility at the next level after he was selected in the fifth round of the NFL Draft by the Chicago Bears. Listed at 5-10 and 190 pounds Azumah was deemed too small to survive the rigors of pro football as a running back so he transitioned to defensive back. He also made the Pro Bowl in 2003 as a kick returner to highlight a seven-year career at the highest level. “He was a natural athlete,” Bowes said. “Let’s face it, he had so much athletic ability he could make the adjustment rather quickly. There’s no question in my mind he would have been a great corner but we couldn’t afford to put him in on defense. We had to have him on offense.” Azumah was inducted into the UNH Athletics Hall of Fame in 2005, but his impact on the local community extended well beyond the football field. “He was a great player,” Bowes said. “There’s no question about it. The thing that I think sets Jerry Azumah apart from other people, he was even a better person. He was a better person than a football player, and he was a great football player. “He was called upon to do so many things to speak to young kids and whatnot,” he added. “I don’t think he ever turned down an appointment like that or a request. He was just a great young man. You can’t say it any other way.” We may earn a commission when you buy through links on this page. title: UNH, HUM, CNC Stocks Rally On Medicare Advantage Rate Surprise - Stocktwits
content: Shares of insurers UnitedHealth Group (UNH), Centene (CNC), Humana (HUM), and Elevance Health (ELV) jumped in Monday’s extended trading hours after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced that the payments to private insurers offering Medicare Advantage plans will increase 2.48% next year. This increase implies $13 billion in additional payments to Medicare insurers for the year, the agency said. “When accounting for estimated risk score trend in MA due to factors such as population changes and coding practices, this amounts to a 4.98% increase,” the agency added. The move came as a surprise since in January, the CMS had proposed a roughly flat increase in payments for private Medicare plans the following year, sending shares of insurers down and wiping out about $100 billion in stock market value. The announcement further comes as a relief to the industry plagued by concerns over rising medical costs. Shares of UNH, CNC, HUM and ELV rallied between 5% and 11% at the time of writing. Shares of Aetna parent CVS Health (CVS) rose by about 6.5% while Molina Healthcare (MOH) stock rose a modest 3%. While UnitedHealth is the largest provider of private Medicare Advantage plans in the U.S., Humana is the second largest. Sentiment around HUM stock, meanwhile, increased from ‘neutral’ to ‘extremely bullish’ territory over the past 24 hours, while message volume rose from ‘normal’ to ‘extremely high’ levels. A Stocktwits user expressed hopes for Wall Street analysts weighing in on the impact of the rate on UNH stock on Tuesday. Yet another user noted that analysts were expecting a lower rate. While UNH stock fell 46% over the past 12 months, HUM stock fell 28%. title: UNH Stock Tracks Hot Monthly Streak: Wall Street Cheers ‘Impressive’ Q2 And Sees Over 20% More Room To Run - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth Group, Inc. (UNH) are headed for their fourth monthly win as Wall Street turns more bullish after a large second-quarter (Q2) earnings beat and a sweeping increase to its 2026 outlook. UNH stock rose 1% on Friday, bringing its monthly gain to nearly 3%, while shares also finished the week marginally higher. BofA called UnitedHealth’s quarter “impressive,” noting that earnings beat consensus by 31% and guidance rose 12%. The firm raised its price target to $512, implying over 20% upside, while reiterating a ‘Buy’ rating and citing a “strong” quarter and broad-based outlook increase. Morgan Stanley was even more bullish, lifting its target to $529, implying a 24% upside. The firm said the Q2 beat and higher 2026 targets “validate its disciplined strategy and establish a stronger base for future growth.” Truist, Oppenheimer and KeyBanc each moved to $500 targets, implying a 17% upside. Truist highlighted top- and bottom-line beats, a better Medical Care Ratio, and improving expectations for UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health. Oppenheimer said that the company “handily” topped expectations, while KeyBanc said results “topped bullish expectations” and argued UnitedHealth could hit $30 in earnings per share (EPS) sooner than anticipated. Goldman Sachs and UBS both raised their targets to $490, implying a 15% upside. Goldman cited a “material” earnings beat, stronger Optum Health profitability and a larger-than-expected guidance increase. UBS said UnitedHealth was “making good progress with more to go.” Meanwhile, RBC Capital raised its target to $478, implying a 12% upside. It remained positive on the earnings beat and guidance hike but flagged investor concern around persistent commercial medical-cost pressure. UnitedHealth posted adjusted EPS of $6.38, beating the $4.92 consensus and rising from $4.08 a year ago. Revenue of $112.03 billion also topped estimates, while the medical care ratio improved to 86.7% from 89.4%. Additionally, the company raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to $19.50-$20 from more than $18.25, lifted UnitedHealthcare’s operating profit forecast to at least $12 billion, and increased Optum Health’s outlook to at least $2.2 billion. CEO Stephen Hemsley said UnitedHealth was “returning to form” as stronger performance disciplines took hold. He reaffirmed the company’s 13%-16% long-term earnings-growth target and doubled the 2026 buyback goal to at least $5 billion. Medicare Advantage drove the beat, with costs coming in below expectations. “Medicare delivered a strong second quarter,” UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said. Commercial plans remained the weak spot, with medical-cost trends above 11%. On the other hand, Optum said its tools added nearly 200,000 patient-facing hours, cut clinician cognitive burnout by 90%, and achieved a 96% first-pass approval rate for digital prior authorizations. SpaceX (SPCX) shares rose 1% overnight heading into Monday after CEO Elon Musk dismissed a report claiming that the rocket and satellite company had placed a $52 billion order with Foxconn for Nvidia-powered AI servers. SPCX stock fell 5% on Friday, extending its weekly decline to 15%. “This is fake news,” Musk said on X in response to a post summarizing the reported agreement. Taiwan’s Economic Daily said that Hon Hai Precision Industry, better known as Foxconn, had secured its first contract to manufacture AI servers for SpaceX. According to the report, SpaceX was preparing to deploy more than 13,000 server racks built around Nvidia’s GB300 platform. Citrini analyst Jukan said on X that Foxconn had displaced the dominance of Dell Technologies and Super Micro Computer in supplying AI server infrastructure to SpaceX. It also claimed deliveries would begin in late 2026 and continue into the first quarter of 2027. Chairman Young Liu has previously said Foxconn expects to capture more than 40% of the global AI server market, while shipments of advanced AI racks are projected to increase through the end of the year. A separate Wall Street Journal report on Friday said that SpaceX was in discussions with the U.S. Department of Defense about supplying data-center capacity worth several billion dollars for military AI workloads. The talks were said to be ongoing and could still fail to produce an agreement. SpaceX has also explored offering computing power to outside AI customers as it seeks to compete more directly with cloud infrastructure providers such as CoreWeave. In June, SpaceX also reached computing arrangements with Google and Anthropic. The Google deal covered access to about 110,000 Nvidia chips, while Anthropic secured capacity at the company’s Colossus 1 data center in Memphis. ATAI stock rose 1% on Friday, adding 40% over the past five sessions and marking its best week in more than a year. Shares, however, were dipping more than 1% in overnight trading heading into Monday. Wood highlighted on X the biotech company’s role in bringing psychedelic medicines closer to mainstream clinical use: “Not only a well-deserved return for ATAI shareholders, this transaction validates Christian’s heartfelt mission and vision,” Wood said. She called Angermayer’s work with ATAI “one of the biggest catalysts of the psychedelic renaissance,” adding that clinical trials are increasingly validating the potential of psychedelics in treatment-resistant depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and broader mental health conditions. Wood also credited Angermayer with backing the field long before psychedelic medicine became widely accepted, fashionable, or investable. “Long before psychedelics were accepted, fashionable, or investable, Christian’s life’s mission was to reactivate them and bring back hope and health for those who had lost both,” she said. Wood’s praise came after ARK Invest reduced its ATAI stake last week. The ARK Genomic Revolution ETF (ARKG) sold 1.12 million ATAI shares worth about $6.02 million. As of Friday, however, ARKG still held 3.19 million shares valued at $22.78 million, or 1.4% of the fund. Lilly was also ARKG’s seventh-largest holding, with 61,258 shares worth $71.62 million and a 4.4% weighting. Eli Lilly said last week that it would acquire AtaiBeckley for up to $3.8 billion for the psychedelic drug developer as it builds out its neuroscience pipeline. Under the deal, shareholders would receive $6.75 in cash per ATAI share, with Lilly committing $2.8 billion at closing and an additional $1 billion for future milestones. The deal marked a 26% premium to AtaiBeckley’s shareholders. The companies are targeting completion of the acquisition in the third quarter of 2026. The centerpiece of the deal is BPL-003, an intranasal psychedelic therapy being tested in late-stage studies for treatment-resistant depression. Jefferies has projected that the drug could eventually generate $1 billion to $2 billion in sales if the program succeeds. AtaiBeckley has said the first late-stage data are expected in early 2029. Angermayer reflected on the deal over the weekend in an X post, saying ATAI’s next phase is about commercialization rather than advocacy. “Ten years ago, psychedelics needed an evangelist. Today, they need commercialization,” he said. After first exploring psychedelics in 2014, Angermayer helped launch Compass Pathways and ATAI in 2017 and invested more than $100 million of his own capital in ATAI. The two companies later raised over $1.5 billion, went public and helped build clinical credibility for psychedelic medicine. title: Quinnipiac hockey opener: big, stunning 10-2 rout of UNH - Total Apex Sports
content: Home > College Sports > Quinnipiac hockey opener: big, stunning 10-2 rout of UNH The Quinnipiac hockey opener was a 10-2 rout of New Hampshire, with four first-period goals and a first win for goalie Christian Kirsch in Hamden. The Quinnipiac hockey opener turned into a rout Friday night, as No. 7 Quinnipiac beat New Hampshire 10-2 before a sellout crowd at M&T Bank Arena in Hamden, Connecticut. The Bobcats scored 10 goals for the first time since 2013, the school said. Quinnipiac scored four times in the first period and led 4-0 after 20 minutes. The Bobcats followed with three goals in the second and three more in the third, according to New Hampshire’s game recap. New Hampshire scored twice in the second period. Freshman Mason Zebeski scored at 13:33, and senior assistant captain Nick Ring scored on the power play at 17:01. Ethan Wyttenbach had two goals and an assist, and Chris Pelosi added two goals. Alex Kostov had two assists in his college debut. Parker Alcos and Dylan Edwards each scored their first collegiate goals, Quinnipiac’s recap said. Goaltender Christian Kirsch earned his first college win with 21 saves on 23 shots. Sixteen Bobcats skaters recorded a point, the most since January 2024. The 10 goals also marked the second-highest total in a season opener in program history, behind a 12-goal game against St. John’s in 1981-82. New Hampshire used two goalies. Michael Simpson made 16 saves, and Teagan Kendrick stopped nine in relief. Quinnipiac hosts Merrimack on Saturday at 4 p.m. EDT at M&T Bank Arena. New Hampshire (0-1) opens Hockey East play at Merrimack on Oct. 8 at 7 p.m., then plays two games at Colgate on Oct. 16-17. Wyttenbach opened the scoring just 2:29 into the game before Tyler Borgula, Dylan Edwards and Matthew Lansing added first-period goals to give Quinnipiac a 4-0 lead after 20 minutes. Braden Blace made it 5-0 just 26 seconds into the second before New Hampshire finally broke through on Mason Zebeski’s goal at 13:33. Pelosi answered with a power-play goal less than two minutes later, and after Nick Ring scored on the power play for the Wildcats at 17:01, Wyttenbach responded just 19 seconds later to send Quinnipiac into the third leading 7-2. The Bobcats added three more in the final period, getting a power-play goal from Mason Marcellus just 16 seconds after the opening faceoff before Parker Alcos and Pelosi closed out the scoring 30 seconds apart midway through the period. Christian Kirsch made 21 saves for Quinnipiac, which finished 2-for-5 on the power play and won 45 of 65 faceoffs. No. 10 Massachusetts became the first ranked team to fall this season, dropping a 2-0 road decision to Colorado College on Friday night. Mats Lindgren scored the only goal Colorado College would need at 14:09 of the first period, and goaltender Jackson Unger made the lead stand up with a 32-save shutout. Massachusetts had three power-play opportunities but could not convert. The Minutemen pushed in the third, outshooting Colorado College 15-13 in the period, but Unger turned aside everything he faced. Drew Montgomery sealed the win with an empty-net goal with 13 seconds remaining. Ethan Eskit was sharp in defeat for Massachusetts, stopping 34 of 35 shots as Colorado College finished with a 36-32 edge in shots. Defending national champion Denver opened its title defense with a 6-2 victory over Alaska Anchorage on Friday night. Tye Spencer gave Alaska Anchorage an early lead just 1:41 into the game, but Daxon Rudolph tied it midway through the first before Denver took control with four goals in the second period. Kieran Cebrian scored shorthanded 1:15 into the period, Cale Ashcroft made it 3-1 at 6:12 and, after Spencer answered on the power play, Sam Harris and Jake Fisher scored 14 seconds apart to push the lead to 5-2. Fisher added his second goal of the night midway through the third. Denver finished with a 39-16 advantage in shots and held Alaska Anchorage to just three shots in the final period. Johnny Hicks made 14 saves for the Pioneers, while William Gramme stopped 33 shots for Alaska Anchorage. Michigan broke open a tie game with three second-period goals and rolled to a 7-2 victory over Bowling Green on Friday night in the season opener for both teams. J.P. Hurlbert gave the Wolverines an early lead at 5:01 of the first period, but Jérémie Minville answered on the power play just over two minutes later to send the teams to the first intermission tied 1-1. Michigan then took control in the second, getting goals from Cole McKinney and Michael Hage 2:14 apart before Jayden Perron made it 4-1 at 12:19. Garrett Schifsky extended the lead just 1:31 into the third before Hage scored his second of the night midway through the period. Maxwell Martin added Bowling Green’s second goal at 13:11, but Malcolm Spence closed the scoring for Michigan with 2:23 remaining. Jack Ivankovic made 29 saves for the Wolverines, including 17 in the third period as Bowling Green generated 18 of its 31 shots over the final 20 minutes. Michigan finished with a 42-31 advantage in shots and scored once on five power-play opportunities. Fresh off its national championship game appearance in April, No. 6 Wisconsin built a three-goal lead through two periods and held off Robert Morris for a 4-2 victory Friday night. Luke Osburn opened the scoring for the Badgers at 17:03 of the first period before Bruno Idzan doubled the lead midway through the second. Dylan Compton then made it 3-0 with a power-play goal at 16:13 as Wisconsin outshot Robert Morris 21-6 in the period and 33-9 through 40 minutes. Robert Morris got on the board on Dominic Elliott’s power-play goal 3:14 into the third, but Finn Brink restored Wisconsin’s three-goal lead with a shorthanded goal at 15:26. George Krotiris scored with two seconds remaining to account for the final margin. Alexis Cournoyer made 16 saves in his Wisconsin debut, while Charlie Schenkel stopped 34 shots for Robert Morris. The Badgers finished with a 38-18 advantage in shots. No. 5 Minnesota Duluth survived a strong challenge from LIU, scoring four times in the third period to pull away for a 7-4 victory Friday night. The Bulldogs led 2-0 after first-period goals from Barrett Hall and Adam Kleber, but LIU answered with three goals in the second. Luc Bydal scored twice in a span of 3:37 before Hunter Anderson briefly restored Minnesota Duluth’s lead. Luca Leighton tied the game at 3-3 with 3:10 remaining in the period. LIU then took its first lead just 3:08 into the third on Brennan Nelson’s goal, but Jayson Shaugabay answered only 12 seconds later. Luke Bibby put Minnesota Duluth back in front for good at 13:57, and Callum Arnott followed 50 seconds later with a power-play goal to make it 6-4. Ty Hanson added a shorthanded empty-net goal with 21 seconds remaining. Minnesota Duluth finished with a 36-23 advantage in shots, while Ethan Dahlmeir made 19 saves for the Bulldogs. After a tumultuous month away from the rink, Arizona State opened its season with a convincing 5-0 victory over Lindenwood on Friday night. The Sun Devils are playing without head coach Greg Powers, who was placed on paid administrative leave this week while the university continues to investigate the Aug. 20 workout in which defenseman Matthew Mayich suffered exertional heat stroke and remains in a coma. Assistant coach Mike Corbett is leading the team in Powers’ absence. Ben Muthersbaugh opened the scoring on the power play at 16:47 of the first period before Kyle Smolen made it 2-0 with 33 seconds remaining in the second. Arizona State then broke the game open in the third, getting goals from Olivier Houde, Sean McGurn and Daniel Shlaine. Samuel Urban stopped all 37 shots he faced to earn the shutout as Lindenwood matched Arizona State with 37 shots. The Sun Devils finished 2-for-5 on the power play and killed all five Lindenwood opportunities. Maryville made an immediate statement in its transition to Division I hockey, rallying from two goals down to stun St. Lawrence, 3-2, Friday night at Appleton Arena. St. Lawrence built a 2-0 lead on Cooper Pierson’s power-play goal at 7:09 of the first period and Luke Posthumus’ goal 5:18 into the second. But Maryville began its comeback late in the middle period when Antoine Dorion scored shorthanded at 18:10. Dorion struck again on the power play at 10:03 of the third to tie the game before Gustavs Ozolins completed the comeback with 1:01 remaining in regulation, giving the Saints their first victory over an NCAA Division I opponent during their transition season. St. Lawrence finished with 29 shots and got 25 saves from Cameron Smith. Dorion led Maryville with two goals and an assist. No. 14 Minnesota at No. 19 Michigan Tech (PPD, poor ice conditions) The only opening-night matchup between nationally ranked teams never got underway Friday, as No. 14 Minnesota’s game at No. 19 Michigan Tech was postponed because of unplayable ice conditions at John MacInnes Student Ice Arena. Michigan Tech cited player safety in making the decision. The series will now begin Saturday at 4:07 p.m. ET, with Friday’s postponed game rescheduled for Sunday at 3:07 p.m. ET. Tynan Lawrence scored 1:18 into overtime to lift No. 16 Boston University past Alaska, 2-1, Friday night. Jack Murtagh gave the Terriers the lead at 3:58 of the first period, but Linden Burrett answered on the power play less than three minutes later. Neither team scored again in regulation despite Boston University finishing with a 39-26 advantage in shots through three periods. Lawrence ended it on BU’s fourth shot of overtime, giving the Terriers the win after assisting on Murtagh’s opening goal. Mikhail Yegorov made 25 saves for Boston University, while Tyler Shea stopped 41 shots for Alaska.

title: USNH Launches New Free Tuition Program For New Hampshire Families Making Up To $100K - Patch
content: A UNH education is now within reach for more New Hampshire families, thanks to the New Hampshire Promise, a new program launched by the University System of New Hampshire. Beginning in fall 2027, incoming first-year and transfer students from families earning up to $100,000 a year can have their tuition covered at any USNH institution, removing a major financial barrier and giving more students the opportunity to pursue their goals and build their future in New Hampshire. “New Hampshire’s public institutions of higher education are a transformative opportunity for students,” USNH Chancellor Cathy Provencher says. “In launching this new program, all of the university system institutions are working together to make higher education more accessible for more New Hampshire students, enabling them to pursue their dreams right here in the Granite State.” Under the terms of the program, New Hampshire residents who are admitted as full-time, first-year students or transfers who have graduated from a New Hampshire community college, with total family income of up to $100,000, qualify to attend a USNH institution — UNH Durham, UNH Manchester, UNH College of Professional Studies Online, Plymouth State University, and Keene State College — tuition-free. With New Hampshire’s median household income of $99,782, according to recent U.S. Census Bureau data, the program has the potential to benefit a significant portion of the state’s families. Admitted students who submit a Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) will automatically be considered for the New Hampshire Promise; there is no separate application process. While the program covers tuition, it does not cover housing, food, books, or fees. “The New Hampshire Promise program is an investment in our students and in the future of our state. By expanding affordable pathways to higher education, we’re creating more opportunities for our young people to pursue good-paying jobs and making it easier for them to build their careers in New Hampshire,” says New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte. “I thank the University System of New Hampshire for their efforts to make college more affordable for New Hampshire students and their families.” The New Hampshire Promise replaces USNH’s Granite Guarantee program, established in 2017 to provide free tuition to Pell-eligible New Hampshire students. Since its inception, more than 4,000 students have qualified for this program. Currently enrolled USNH undergraduates will remain in Granite Guarantee to ensure no disruption of financial aid benefits. The program is the latest effort to make college more affordable in the Granite State. Last month, the University of New Hampshire announced that it awarded a record $40 million in financial aid to incoming students this year, with the average student award topping $16,000. Almost every student in the incoming class (96%) received financial aid, with an average award of $16,918, an increase of more than 50% from the prior year. These efforts, combined with UNH’s high student success rates, led to UNH being named New England’s No. 1 best value public university for the sixth consecutive year, according to the Best Value Schools rankings of National Universities by U.S. News & World Report. According to UNH’s most recent graduating class survey data, UNH graduates boast a 94% success rate, with 71.6% of students employed within 12 months after graduation and another 22.2% enrolled in further education. Additionally, the significant majority of employed graduates — 88% — reported that their job was directly or somewhat related to their major.

title: UNH officials say rise in reported rape cases could show more survivors are coming forward - WMUR
content: The new investigation of an alleged rape at Cornell University is drawing attention to college campuses across the country and how they handle assault allegations. The recent Security and Fire Safety Report at the University of New Hampshire shows that reported rape cases are up on and off campus, but the school and advocates argue that could show their efforts to connect victims to resources are working. "As a woman myself, it's terrifying to think about," said UNH sophomore Tess Vallas. Students at UNH said the reports coming out of Cornell University are hard to hear. >> Download the free WMUR app to get updates on the go << "Honestly, it's just really disappointing," said UNH freshman Madeline Dowling. They said it's also hard to hear that their school is reporting a rise in rape cases in the past three years. There were 26 cases reported in 2023, 41 in 2024 and 46 in 2025. "I don't see why that wouldn't be a concern for anyone," Vallas said. "It's not good," said UNH sophomore Tristan White. "It doesn't help either party in the end." UNH said it takes such crimes very seriously and has increased its training to make sure victims have the best support available. School officials said they believe those efforts are why the rape case reports are rising, because more survivors feel comfortable coming forward and not necessarily because more crimes are occurring. UNH offers resources through its SHARPP Center for Interpersonal Violence Awareness, Prevention and Advocacy on campus and partners with the state's Coalition Against Domestic and Sexual Violence to help victims navigate what follows after making a report. "An advocate can help walk a survivor through what each of those are going to look like and what their options are," said Emily Provencher, prevention and child welfare specialist. Those services are available 24/7 and offer a confidential advocate who helps survivors explore their next steps, such as filing a criminal or Title IX complaint or doing nothing at all. Provencher said they're trained to offer the support a survivor needs. "They're going to center everything on what you want and what works best for you," she said. The coalition said that after reports like the Cornell investigation come out, it sees an increase in calls to the center from survivors who feel they can step up after seeing other survivors come forward. If you or someone you know is a victim of sexual abuse, you can call the state's 24/7 sexual assault hotline at 866-644-3574 to be connected with resources. title: UNH Dunkin' Mural: Artist Hides Self-Portrait at MUBkin - Hoodline
content: A massive new mural now stretches across the Dunkin' inside the University of New Hampshire's Memorial Union Building, and if you look closely enough, you might spot the artist herself tucked into the scene wearing a cap and gown. Madeline Pender, a UNH alumna, was hired by Dunkin' to envision and paint the artwork as part of a redesign that turns the beloved campus coffee shop into the chain's first college-campus Signature Series store in New England. Pender painted the mural, which spans the length of the Dunkin' store. She included a self-portrait tucked into the scene. The mural, unveiled Thursday at the Dunkin' location inside the Memorial Union Building, features UNH student athletes, Thomson Hall, the Wildcat statue, and students clutching coffee and donuts, per the same account. It's a fitting tribute for a space students have long called their own. The Memorial Union Building's Dunkin' is so central to daily life on campus that students have nicknamed it “MUBkin,” according to the University of New Hampshire. The store is a familiar campus fixture, and Dunkin' chose it for its signature redesign. Pender also depicted Eli Bryant, a 2024 UNH alumnus and one of her closest friends, standing at an easel inside the mural, according to the Globe's reporting. The artwork he's shown painting on his easel depicts a waterfaring vessel built by UNH students. DriX is an autonomous surface vessel; UNH's Center for Coastal and Ocean Mapping has housed and supported DriX vessels since December 2018, according to UNH's Center for Coastal and Ocean Mapping. The campus landmarks woven throughout the mural carry their own histories. Thomson Hall, one of the primary buildings rendered in the artwork, is a Romanesque structure at the center of campus listed on the National Register of Historic Places, according to Society19. The Wildcat statue is another campus icon featured in the mural. The Memorial Union Building is the setting for the mural. Pender worked with Dunkin' and UNH representatives through several mural iterations before the final design came together, the Globe reports. She hand-painted the design elements herself, and the artwork was then assembled as a digital collage and printed onto the wall covering. The project marks the first Dunkin' Signature Series store on a college campus in New England, per Dunkin'. Pender said senior year was the first time campus life started to feel normal again, the Globe reports, a detail that adds personal weight to her return to UNH as both teacher and muralist. Her mural leaves a lasting imprint at UNH. Pender's mural brings new artwork to the Memorial Union Building. The MUBkin is now home to Dunkin's Signature Series store and Pender's mural. The sprawling mural gives the campus coffee shop a distinctive new look, with a UNH alumna's own face now watching over the counter. title: Physicist Receives Grant Through Department of Energy’s Competitive Genesis Mission - University of New Hampshire
content: Nathaly Santiesteban, assistant professor of physics and astronomy. UNH physicist Nathaly Santiesteban has received funding from the Department of Energy’s highly competitive Genesis Mission to explore using artificial intelligence to better understand spin and the fundamental structure of matter, addressing questions at the heart of modern nuclear physics. Santiesteban’s project was one of just 278 selected from over 5,000 proposals to the Genesis Mission, which aims to accelerate breakthroughs and double the nation’s scientific productivity with AI-enabled workflows. “This research addresses a fundamental question: How does matter acquire the properties we observe? Most visible matter is made of protons and neutrons, yet we still do not fully understand how their internal components produce properties such as spin,” says Santiesteban, assistant professor of physics and astronomy. Santiesteban’s project will use artificial intelligence to make polarized-target systems — specialized experimental setups used in nuclear and particle physics to align the spin axes of atomic nuclei — easier to operate, more reliable, and more responsive to changing experimental conditions. She and her UNH co-principal investigators, Karl Slifer, professor of physics and astronomy, and Elena Long, associate professor of physics and astronomy, will use the polarized-target laboratory at UNH as the project’s primary testing site. Funded with $750,000 for the first nine-month phase and up to $15 million for the three-year phase two, Santiesteban will collaborate with researchers from the Department of Energy’s Jefferson Lab and the University of Virginia, the University of Tennessee, and New Mexico State University. Karl Slifer, professor of physics and astronomy and Elena Long, associate professor of physics and astronomy, will collaborate with Santiesteban (center) on UNH's Genesis Mission project. Polarized-target systems are highly complex. They operate at temperatures lower than those of outer space and combine powerful magnetic fields, microwaves, sophisticated radio-frequency equipment, and materials that require strict safety controls. Scientists direct a particle beam at the polarized material and study how the particles scatter. “The project could also demonstrate how AI can work safely with complex scientific equipment, with potential applications in other laboratories and advanced technologies,” Santiesteban says. “Running these experiments at research facilities is very demanding because every part of the system must be continuously monitored and carefully controlled to achieve and maintain the desired polarization. Our project aims to reduce the amount of manual intervention required and increase experimental efficiency by using artificial intelligence to monitor the system and optimize its operating variables in real time.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: Food among the trees - University of New Hampshire
content: New Hampshire is more than 80% forested, second ‌in coverage only to Maine in the U.S. The Adaptive ‌Agroforestry Principles and Teaching (ADAPT) program is leveraging this important resource through the testing and teaching of agroforestry concepts and methods, work that will support local farming and sustain a stronger regional food system. Agroforestry expands agricultural opportunities by embracing, rather than seeking to overcome, the tree-filled landscape. ADAPT is a collaborative effort led by Heidi Asbjornsen, professor of natural resources and the environment, that also includes researchers at Yale University, Dartmouth College, and 12 operating farms. ADAPT works with three primary types of agroforestry. Forest farming grows shade-tolerant crops under an existing tree canopy. Food forests contain food-producing plants of varying heights, such as nut trees, berry bushes, and herbs, within the same space. And silvopasture provides livestock pasturing and grazing space among trees. Unlike most fully cleared pasture and crop lands, all offer welcoming habitats for beneficial insects, pollinators, and wildlife. “Agroforestry can increase crop diversity and sustainability, providing farmers and growers with more resilience in changing conditions as well as expanding income-generating opportunities,” says Asbjornsen. “But agroforestry systems are complex to manage. Education and extension are critical parts of ADAPT so that we can share our research-based insights with the community.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: What Can You Do With an OTD? One Graduate’s Capstone Shows the Possibilities - University of New Hampshire
content: While working as a nanny in high school, Sarah Morrison ‘24 ‘26G watched a child participate in occupational therapy and became curious about the profession. The more she learned, the more she realized it aligned perfectly with her interests in healthcare. “The ability to work in a variety of settings, and the privilege to assist individuals of all ages to accomplish tasks that are meaningful to them, was exactly what I wanted,” Morrison says. Morrison, of Westwood, Massachusetts, entered UNH's occupational therapy program directly from high school, beginning a pathway that would ultimately lead to her occupational therapy doctorate (OTD). She graduated from the program's first cohort and now works as a travel occupational therapist. UNH’s first occupational therapy doctorate graduating cohort. Prospective occupational therapy students often ask whether they should pursue a master's degree or a doctoral degree. Both pathways prepare graduates to become licensed occupational therapists. The OTD includes additional advanced study and a doctoral capstone, allowing students to deepen their expertise through experiences in leadership, research, advocacy, teaching, and program development. For Morrison, that opportunity to go deeper was a major reason she pursued the OTD. "Earning my OTD was important to me because it gave me the opportunity to go above and beyond with a capstone project and really dive into something that was specific to my interests," she says. “Additionally, it provided me the opportunity to work as a graduate assistant, teaching labs and courses, working on research projects, and really get to know the ins and outs of how academia works.” Morrison's clinical experiences included a placement at a Level I trauma center in Boston, which gave her experience in the acute-care setting. Her capstone allowed her to explore another area of interest: the connection between physical recovery and mental health. Patients recovering from serious illness or injury can also experience anxiety, depression, trauma, and other forms of psychological distress. Research reviewed as part of Morrison's project suggested that leaving those concerns unaddressed can contribute to poorer physical and functional outcomes. Morrison's capstone, Connecting Minds and Bodies: Advancing Mental Health Support Through Occupational Therapy in Acute Care Environments, focused on helping occupational therapists better address those needs. Partnering with Portsmouth Regional Hospital, Morrison developed resources to make mental health screening and intervention more accessible in hospital settings. Morrison conducted a national survey of occupational therapists working in inpatient settings to better understand how confident and competent they felt addressing mental health concerns among physically ill and injured patients. She found that while many therapists felt capable of supporting patients' mental health needs, barriers such as limited time, productivity requirements, inadequate resources, and competing clinical demands often made it difficult to do so consistently. “My program development was a combination of a screening tool and intervention ideas that fell within the OT scope of practice that could be utilized by OTs in this setting to address this particular need of our patients to hopefully mitigate some of the long-term effects,” Morrison says. “It also had educational handouts for patients, caregivers, and other healthcare disciplines on how we can all address this need.” The results of Morrison’s capstone were encouraging. Following implementation of the program, therapists reported feeling better equipped to address mental health needs, and documentation showed increased screening and intervention efforts in this area. After graduation, Morrison accepted a position as a travel occupational therapist in Montana. Morrison says the additional experiences she gained through the OTD helped prepare her to pursue travel therapy as a new graduate. “I know that I will eventually want to transition to an academic role while practicing per diem so that I can offer valuable learning experiences to future occupational therapy students the same way my professors did for me,” Morrison says. “The real-world experience they all brought to the classroom was an added layer of expertise and quality of learning that I think all classrooms should have” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: NH’s public colleges will waive tuition for eligible students - New Hampshire Public Radio
content: Beginning next year, certain students will get free tuition at New Hampshire's state colleges. To be eligible, students must be New Hampshire residents, meet certain academic requirements and be attending one of the schools for the first time. Their families cannot earn more than $100,000 a year. The University System of New Hampshire announced the program, The New Hampshire Promise, Thursday. In a statement, Gov. Kelly Ayotte said tuition waivers will be good for students and employers. “By expanding affordable pathways to higher education, we’re creating more opportunities for our young people to pursue good-paying jobs and making it easier for them to build their careers in New Hampshire,” she said. Under a prior version of the program, which was tied to federal loan eligibility requirements, nearly 4,000 students received tuition waivers between 2017 and this academic year. Tania deLuzuriaga, a University of New Hampshire spokesperson, said they estimate the change in eligibility requirements will mean an additional 29% of next year’s incoming class will qualify for the program. Under the prior program, students had to complete a lengthy and complicated federal Pell Grant application before they knew whether they would qualify for federal aid. That can be a hurdle, deLuzuriaga said, especially for first-generation students whose family members have not navigated the process before. Now, students know up front whether they qualify and only need to fill out the standard federal financial aid application. New Hampshire's public colleges and universities lost nearly $20 million in the last state budget. That prompted UNH to cut $17.5 million from its budget, leading to staff cuts and a hiring freeze. Student enrollment has also been declining. Kimberly DeRego, chief enrollment officer for the University System of New Hampshire, said in an email that the schools will pay for the tuition waivers with money from its endowment. The University System also hopes the new program will attract donors who want to support lower-income students. Students can enroll at UNH, Plymouth State University, Keene State College and UNH’s College of Professional Studies online program, and do not have to live on campus. They must have earned at least a 2.7 GPA at their prior school and be a full-time student. The waivers could save students between $12,000 and $16,000 a year in tuition, depending on where they enroll. Tuition for UNH’s College of Professional Studies costs about $7,700 a year. Students will still have to pay for room and board and fees. The tuition waiver is available only to first-year students and transfer students who have earned an associate's degree at one of the state’s community colleges. It is not open to current students unless they are receiving tuition waivers under the prior program. Students will continue receiving tuition waivers throughout their college degree as long as they continue to meet the eligibility requirements. Students do not have to apply to be considered. The University System will use information from the federal student loan application to determine if they are eligible. Saint Anselm College in Manchester began its own tuition waiver program last year for New Hampshire and Maine students. Last month, it announced it was explaining eligibility to Vermont students.
